name: Yusuf Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At 58 I play hand percussion for a touring folk trio, record short rhythm tracks and teach adults at a college. I have a music degree and know the beat well, yet loading drums after the last bus is hard on my back. I like the moment when three players breathe together and the room starts moving.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is the money situation at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs kitchen machines and our children have left home. We have a mortgage, barely two weeks of expenses saved, lower pay than most players I know and few nearby bands with paid openings. I use AI every day to sort my own demo clips, but I listen back before anyone pays for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the trio that a tidy booking sheet helps only if the player fee and van share are written beside each date. I would still count every drum in before we leave the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even in a plateau, a cancelled weekend leaves us near the mortgage line. Two weeks of savings is barely a bridge from one paid show to the next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the trio, paid college classes and rhythm-track clients, and ask for the next three show fees and travel shares in writing. In the plateau’s first year I would request an actual pension estimate and compare it with our bills before even discussing a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a quiet weekend already. A clean calendar cannot fill the van with paid dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know what the pension would be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have never requested the figure. I cannot put an imagined pension on the mortgage ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you do if a venue cancels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the written cancellation term and call the clients with paid recording work. Few bands nearby have a spare paid chair.

I would welcome a **tidier calendar** with paid dates visible.
think: A **cancelled weekend** threatens the mortgage because our paid trio calendar has gaps between venues.
Our **two-week reserve** cannot cover many quiet weekends, and nearby paid bands are scarce.
do: Keep **trio shows**, college classes and paid rhythm clients this month.
Request **three written show fees**, van shares and cancellation terms.
Request an **actual pension estimate** in the plateau’s first year and compare it with bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current income gaps.

fieldNote: His **two-week reserve** and lower musician pay leave ordinary venue cancellations painful even in a plateau.
He wants an **actual pension estimate** before discussing any retirement date, while he keeps paid trio and college work.

Request actual pension estimate in first plateau year; compare with bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell recording clients that a generated drum loop may be cheap, but a live trio still needs paid players. I would ask which studio calls remain on the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third of my own income comes from short rhythm tracks. I expect some clients to buy generated loops, and our two-week reserve will not carry a lost third for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would request written studio and trio dates and a paid engineer lesson on a new stem checker, which separates sounds in a recording. In disruption’s first year I would test only my own nameless drum take with a studio-funded licence permitting paid use and approved local studio storage, without losing paid sessions, compare every beat with the source by ear, and stop if timing changes or the file leaves the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing track fees. Learning the stem checker might help me catch errors, but it cannot create a paying client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test it on a learner’s take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A pupil’s voice and name stay in the college folder; my own recording is enough for a trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the engineer has no paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid studio work and wait for a funded lesson. I will not trade a paid session for a free demonstration.

feel: I feel **anxious** about likely lost recording fees.
S1.quote: Learning the stem checker might help me catch errors, but it cannot create a paying client.
fieldNote: The **new stem checker** needs paid instruction, approved local storage, owned nameless audio and manual listening.
His **recording third** is exposed while the household holds only two weeks of savings.

steps.text: Request written studio and trio dates plus paid engineer lesson next month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the trio that thinking AGI in 2028 could price my recorded rhythms down before robots can strike a drum around 2031. I would ask venues to sign the live fees now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the paid loop orders to end in 2028, and one venue may replace our set with a backing track. Losing a third of my pay is enough to make the mortgage sums wake me at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would total the last six months of loop invoices and secure signed trio dates. In the first year after 2028, if loop orders end and live fees also fall, I would apply for a posted paid arts-centre music technician job only if its requirements accept my music degree and stage setup experience, the written net offer after travel replaces lost fees, and the last bus works; I would keep paid trio and college hours until that offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the expected loss of loop orders and a possible venue cut. I can search, but there are few paid posts near home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the music degree guarantee a technician job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The actual posting has to accept both my degree and my stage setup work. I would not leave a paid trio for a job that exists only in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you say 2031 for robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is when the card places capable hands-on robots, three years after thinking AGI. A recorded loop price can collapse in 2028 without a robot drummer.

Keep **trio and college hours** until a signed offer and workable last bus.

S2.quote: Losing a third of my pay is enough to make the mortgage sums wake me at night.
fieldNote: The **loop third** is expected to disappear in 2028, before hands-on robots in 2031.
A **technician posting** must accept his degree and setup experience and pay replacement net after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the venue that five years until AGI by 2031 is enough to learn live sound safely if training hours are paid. Robot drummers around 2034 are a later problem than recorded loop fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect loop sales to thin before 2031, and I cannot pay for a sound course out of two weeks of savings. A technician role might suit my stage work, but a course certificate is not an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would enrol in a live-sound certificate only after a venue confirms a real funded place, paid training hours without lost college or trio income, a last bus home and written acceptance of that certificate for its posted paid assistant role. In the first year after 2031, if loop or live fees fall, I would apply only if the completed certificate meets that actual posting and a written net offer after travel replaces lost fees; I would keep paid music until a signed offer and do first sound checks under a venue technician, never running a crowded show alone before signed equipment and safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the lost recording trade, but a funded course gives me something to do. I cannot call a live-sound certificate wages until a venue pays for my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you run the mixing desk alone after class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The venue technician would supervise my first checks. I would wait for signed equipment and safety checks before taking a crowded show alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if tuition is free but class time is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would decline that intake and keep the trio and college fees. Free tuition still costs a paid afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that a decade until AGI by 2036 gives us time to put player fees and travel shares on paper. Robot drummers around 2039 do not excuse an unpaid rehearsal today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be playing fewer late nights at 68, but I have no retirement figure and no date set. Loop fees may end by 2036, and two weeks saved still leave our mortgage exposed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate, signed paid trio and college dates, and save five percent of each extra paid festival fee after mortgage, food, van and train costs toward one month of bills. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid teaching and live sets and, if loop fees fall, seek a posted paid arts-centre percussion coordinator role only if it accepts my music degree and teaching record, the written net pay after travel replaces any lost loop fees, and the last bus works; I would keep current paid hours until a new contract is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about what happens when recorded loops stop paying. Ten years before AGI in 2036 gives me time to check contracts, not a spare month in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra festival fee arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I save nothing new from festivals. The one-month cushion is a goal, not money we have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pension estimate change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would set the actual figure beside our bills and health. I would not stop paid work because a statement arrived.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the loop orders could stop before a new venue pays for me. Signed live dates, an actual posted technician vacancy accepting my degree and a written offer after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays a musician while he learns sound. A funded course with unpaid afternoons can still take food off our table.

headlineQuote: A funded course with unpaid afternoons can still take food off our table.
portrait: Yusuf is an **experienced percussionist** with a music degree, paid trio dates, recordings and college classes.
His **lower pay**, two-week reserve, mortgage and few nearby bands make lost recording fees dangerous.
He uses **AI daily** but learns a new stem checker only with paid instruction, approved storage and ear checks.
His **sound course** needs funded paid hours and employer recognition before any application for posted work.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could end loop orders before he finds replacement paid venue work.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **signed live dates**, a posted technician vacancy accepting his degree and written replacement net pay after travel.
